questions.question: YOU are the Provider (83-year-old woman, lightheadedness and nausea): What are the components of a radio report to the hospital?
choices: In order: the patient's full name and address; insurance information; a detailed past medical history; every set of vital signs taken; a list of all medications; and your estimated billing code for the call.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (86-year-old woman, fall into bathtub): With the patient’s history of diabetes, what else might play a role in your care? How does this disease affect the patient’s perception of pain?
choices: Diabetes mainly affects wound care after transport; it has no effect on pain perception, circulation, or blood glucose during a call of this length.
Diabetes heightens pain perception, so her reported pain likely overstates her injuries; her glucose is also unlikely to change after only a few hours without food, so it does not need checking.

Diabetic peripheral neuropathy blunts pain perception, so her injuries (possible hip or pelvis fracture, with crepitus noted) may be worse than her reported pain suggests; assess beyond the pain score. Her diabetes is unrelated to this fall, since it is controlled by diet alone and does not affect sensation in the extremities.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (83-year-old woman, lightheadedness and nausea): Should your general approach to the assessment process be any different for this patient versus a younger patient? Why or why not?

Yes. Assume an older patient's complaints are less reliable, so base the assessment mainly on family reports and your own observations.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (86-year-old woman, fall into bathtub): What are the primary reasons that a prearrival radio report is given to the receiving hospital?
choices: So the dispatcher can close out the call record and the crew can avoid giving a report in person when they arrive.
To obtain permission to transport the patient and to have the hospital assign the crew a room number before they leave the scene.

So the hospital can prepare before you arrive: the right room, staff, and equipment, and activation of any specialty resources. The report gives your ETA, the patient's age and sex, chief complaint, condition and vital signs, and treatment so far, which shortens the time to definitive care.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (86-year-old woman, fall into bathtub): Is it ever justifiable to misinform a patient to reduce the patient’s anxiety temporarily?
choices: No. Never lie to a patient or invent an answer. Misinformation breaks the patient's trust, can distort her decisions about her own care, and creates ethical and legal exposure. Reduce anxiety with honest reassurance and clear explanations instead.
Yes, but only when the patient is elderly or confused, because accurate information would upset them more than it helps.
Yes. If the truth would raise the patient's anxiety, withholding or softening it is considered part of therapeutic communication.
Yes. A small, harmless exaggeration is acceptable if it keeps the patient calm and cooperative during transport.

The caller's insurance information and the patient's preferred hospital first, then the patient's full medication list and the name of her personal physician.

Nature of the illness and scene safety first: possible infectious disease (PPE), environmental hazards such as odors or carbon monoxide (fire department), or a psychiatric emergency with violence risk (law enforcement). Then whether the patient is conscious and breathing adequately, plus age and sex if possible. The more information gathered before arrival, the better prepared you are.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (83-year-old woman, lightheadedness and nausea): How can you maximize successful communication with a patient who is hard of hearing?
choices: First determine the degree of hearing loss; hearing aids may let her hear normally. Do not assume deafness or low intelligence. Position yourself so she can see your lips and facial expressions; never shout in her ear. Ask short questions and give short answers, and listen carefully. If aids fail, a stethoscope in her ears while you speak into the diaphragm can amplify sound. If speech fails, write questions down; a family member may interpret, and basic sign language ('hurt,' 'sick,' 'help') helps.
Rely mainly on her family to answer for her, because direct communication with a hearing-impaired patient is usually unsuccessful.
Avoid written notes and gestures, since they can confuse older patients; instead, keep explanations brief and move on if she does not respond.
Speak as loudly as possible directly into her ear, since volume is the main barrier, and repeat each question several times until she answers.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (83-year-old woman, lightheadedness and nausea): What techniques can facilitate the process of interviewing an older patient?
choices: Limit the interview to yes-or-no questions, avoid eye contact so the patient does not feel pressured, and finish as quickly as possible.
Stand over the patient while asking questions, avoid touch, and discuss the patient's condition with your partner in front of her to save time.

Look directly at the patient and speak slowly and distinctly. Do not raise your volume unless the patient has hearing loss. Use nonverbal communication clues and touch as appropriate. Never talk about the patient in front of her; it implies she has no say in her care and can escalate her fear of losing independence.
Speak quickly and raise your volume so the patient can follow along, and direct most questions to family members who can answer more clearly.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (86-year-old woman, fall into bathtub): What questions do you anticipate emergency department personnel to ask?
choices: Mostly administrative questions: her insurance carrier, her preferred pharmacy, the name of her employer, and who will pay for the transport.

How long she was in the tub and how she was extricated; her mental and neuro status; signs of hypothermia and what warming was done; her blood glucose; medications, allergies, and last food or medication; pulse, motor, and sensory function after immobilization; and any other injuries found.
Questions about your agency's protocols, staffing, and response times rather than the patient's condition.
Only questions about the radio report itself, such as your unit number and the time you left the scene.
